title: RL Environments at Scale – Will Brown, Prime Intellect
talk_summary: Will Brown argues that 'environments' (a harness + tasks + rewards) are the right abstraction for evals, synthetic data, and RL, and that building them forces scientific measurement instead of vibe-checking. He demos the verifiers toolkit and Environments Hub, where a small Qwen3-4B model trained with RL on a wiki-search environment went from 55% to 89%, matching much larger models.

takeaways.what_they_do: Package the agent harness, a task dataset, and a composable reward rubric into one versioned, runnable unit so evals, synthetic data, and training all share the same definition of 'what the agent should do'.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the environment forces you to also have your tasks and your rewards predefined to be able to do this experimentation. It's a proper eval.

takeaways.technique: Composable reward rubric with separate observability metrics
takeaways.what_they_do: Split rewards into a rubric of composable pieces, and allow zero-weight metrics purely for observability of what the agent did.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a rubric is the abstraction for managing the different pieces of your rewards where you can kind of compose different things. You can also have metrics that are just a zero award but are for in uh observability

takeaways.what_they_do: Use a well-defined environment to tune/select models, showing small cheap models can be pushed to match much larger ones on a narrow task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we started with a a Quen 3 4B model, which was about 55%. And after training, it was at 89% on par with uh much larger models
takeaways.numbers: Qwen3-4B: 55% -> 89%, on par with GPT-4.1 and GPT-5-mini

takeaways.technique: Environment as the entry point for all model work
takeaways.what_they_do: Standardize on one artifact (the environment) as the entry point for evals, synthetic data generation, SFT, and RL, so teams don't rebuild infra per use case.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If you want to do synthetic data and SFT build, let's build an environment. If you want to do your evals, you build that as an environment.

takeaways.what_they_do: Build environments hierarchically (base env -> multi-turn -> CLI agent -> specific benchmark) so foundational pieces are reused and special cases compose on top.
takeaways.evidence_quote: thinking of these things hierarchically allows us to kind of really determine like what are the foundational pieces what is generic across all environments
